document_title: DARPA's Triage Challenge finals at TEEX's Disaster City in College Station tested drones and ground robots that find simulated casualties for human medics
_note: Caption carried verbatim from caption_winner.txt. Slide strings polished from storyboard.md, each held to its claim quotes in claims.json. The only figure not in a claim quote is plate_usd from figures.json, a drawing rule.
caption:
Disaster City was built to collapse.

TEEX's 52 acre mock community in College Station even has a derailed train. From November 5th to November 13th it hosted DARPA's Triage Challenge finals. Drones and ground robots worked beside first responders, relaying data on simulated casualties to human medics. RoboScout won the Systems competition and $1.5 million. Disruptors won the Data competition and $1 million.

DARPA Director Stephen Winchell said human machine teams outperform every approach to the problem. Then he said, "But that's not enough, right?" Some teams did well identifying victims. Others did well at triage or evacuation.

DARPA's SBIR topic TRIAGE-X seeks systems that recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the antidote or a life saving intervention. It is open until November 25th. Who in Texas answers it by then?

#DisasterCity #CollegeStation #TEEX

S2.headline: A town built to fall down
S2.body: Disaster City is a 52 acre mock community with full scale structures that can collapse, rubble piles and a derailed train. The layout here is drawn to illustrate and is not the site plan.

S3.headline: Five ways to make it hard
S3.body: The five competitions included a simulated tornado ripping through a community market, smoke filled buildings, nighttime searches in near darkness and search and rescue under piles of rubble. Each set is drawn to illustrate.

S4.headline: Find them. Read them. Tell a medic.
S4.body: Systems had to locate casualties, identify signs of injury and send critical data to medical response teams. Teams built technology to read vital signs from a distance. Moulage artists made hyper realistic mock injuries. Drawn to illustrate.

S5.headline: It searched through the blast
S5.body: On the Human Machine Teaming night course a robot searched for casualties during a controlled explosion while role players took cover. Each team worked with assigned medics. The course simulated an attack on a forward operating base.

S6.headline: More than 100 people competed
S6.body: Participants came from the U.S. military, universities, tech companies and startups. Each badge is one participant, drawn to illustrate.

S7.headline: $1.5 million and $1 million
S7.body: More than $3 million in cash prizes was on offer. RoboScout won the Systems competition and $1.5 million. Disruptors won the Data competition and $1 million. One plate stands for $100,000, drawn to illustrate.

S8.headline: Human machine teams beat every approach. Still not enough.
S8.body: DARPA Director Stephen Winchell said human machine teams outperform every approach to the problem. Then he said that result was not enough. Some teams did well at identifying victims and others at triage, lifesaving or evacuation. DARPA created the challenge in 2023.

S9.headline: The next ask is delivery
S9.body: DARPA's open SBIR topic TRIAGE-X seeks autonomous medical triage systems that recognize chemical toxidromes and physically deliver the antidote or a life saving intervention. It is open until November 25th. The case is drawn to illustrate.
